briefing.headline: Brexit reset, US court clash and party rebellions dominate politics
briefing.overview: Britain’s prime minister says the current Brexit deal has failed and outlines a new EU strategy. In the US, former president Trump attacks a judge’s order halting his golf project, while internal party disputes surface on both sides of the Atlantic.

stories.title: PM calls for Brexit reset ahead of EU summit
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that the Brexit arrangement ‘has not worked’ and set conditions for a new UK‑EU deal. The speech precedes a summit with EU leaders later this week.
stories.why_it_matters: The issue links to the A‑level study of the executive’s role in shaping foreign policy and constitutional change. It also illustrates how the cabinet can drive policy shifts within the uncodified constitution.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Burnham’s reset could restore economic ties and give the UK more influence in European regulation.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: Opponents warn the new deal may compromise sovereignty and repeat past negotiation failures.

perspectives.label: From the right
perspectives.text: Conservative commentators see the reset as a pragmatic correction to a flawed Brexit.

key_term.definition: The branch of government headed by the prime minister that implements laws and conducts foreign policy.

stories.exam_use: Use as evidence of how the executive can initiate constitutional change in an essay on the UK’s uncodified constitution.

stories.title: Labour MPs rebel over Rosebank oilfield plans
stories.what_happened: At least 75 Labour MPs signed a letter opposing the government’s Rosebank oilfield development, with expectations that up to 100 may join. The rebellion reflects wider discontent over Europe and welfare reforms.
stories.why_it_matters: Shows intra‑party dissent, a key concept in the study of political parties and parliamentary democracy. Highlights how backbenchers can influence policy decisions.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: The rebellion protects environmental standards and challenges unchecked fossil‑fuel expansion.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: Proponents claim the project secures jobs and energy security for the UK.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Labour’s left wing sees the move as a stand for climate justice.

key_term.definition: When MPs not holding ministerial office collectively oppose their party leadership.

stories.exam_use: Cite as evidence of party cohesion challenges in an essay on the UK party system.

stories.title: Trump attacks judge’s halt to golf project
stories.what_happened: Former President Donald Trump criticised a judge who ordered a two‑week suspension of his Washington golf development, calling the court’s condition ‘terrible’. He said his administration will appeal the decision.
stories.why_it_matters: Illustrates the tension between the executive and the judiciary, a core theme in the US Constitution study. Highlights judicial review and executive responses.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Trump’s supporters view the halt as political bias against him.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: Legal analysts say the judge is enforcing environmental and zoning laws.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Progressive voices see the appeal as an attempt to sidestep accountability.

key_term.definition: The power of courts to assess the legality of executive actions.

stories.exam_use: Use to discuss checks and balances in a US Constitution essay.

stories.title: Alaska voters reject changes to primary system
stories.what_happened: In the November 3 election, Alaskans voted against a measure to repeal open primaries and ranked‑choice voting, keeping the current system intact for a second time in two years.
stories.why_it_matters: Relevant to the study of US electoral systems and direct democracy. Shows voter attitudes toward electoral reform.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Proponents of the repeal say open primaries dilute party identity.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: Opponents claim the current system encourages broader participation and reduces partisanship.

perspectives.label: From the centre
perspectives.text: Analysts note the repeated rejections reflect satisfaction with existing voting methods.

key_term.definition: A primary election in which voters are not required to be affiliated with a political party.

stories.exam_use: Reference when comparing US primary structures in an essay on electoral reforms.

stories.title: Welsh Labour reaffirms devolution demands
stories.what_happened: Welsh Labour politician Ken Skates said the party remains committed to expanding Senedd powers, including control over the crown estate and policing. This follows criticism that Labour had abandoned these promises.
stories.why_it_matters: Connects to the A‑level focus on devolution and the distribution of powers within the UK constitution. Highlights party positioning on regional authority.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Devolution advocates see the pledge as a step toward greater Welsh self‑government.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: Skeptics warn that further devolution could fragment UK governance.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Labour’s left wing views it as fulfilling progressive decentralisation.

key_term.definition: The statutory transfer of powers from the central UK government to regional bodies.

stories.exam_use: Use as evidence of how parties influence constitutional change in a devolution essay.

compare.uk: The UK prime minister is using a major speech to propose a new EU relationship, showing executive leadership in foreign policy without a written constitution.
compare.us: Former US president Trump publicly attacks a judicial decision, illustrating executive opposition to the judiciary within a codified constitutional framework.
compare.insight: The contrast shows how executive power is exercised differently: the UK relies on political persuasion and parliamentary support, while the US features formal checks by an independent judiciary.

ideas_lens.text: Burnham’s Brexit reset reflects liberal ideas of free trade and individual economic liberty, echoing Adam Smith’s market principles. Conversely, the US court clash raises liberal concerns about protecting individual rights against governmental overreach.

exam_question.question: Assess the extent to which executive actions can shape constitutional change in the UK and the US.
exam_question.tip: Compare the UK prime minister’s policy speech with the US president’s challenge to a judicial ruling, using specific examples.
